title: Earache
meta_description: Find out about earache and ear pain, a common condition, particularly in young children. It's not usually a sign of anything serious, but it can be painful.

structured_data_json_ld.description: Find out about earache and ear pain, a common condition, particularly in young children. It's not usually a sign of anything serious, but it can be painful.

hasPart.description: If you have earache, you may also have other symptoms, such as a high temperature or hearing loss. Earache can be harder to spot in young children.

hasPart.text:
A young child might have earache if they:

  • rub or pull their ear
  • do not react to some sounds
  • have a temperature of 38C or above
  • are irritable or restless
  • are off their food
  • keep losing their balance

Earache and ear pain can affect 1 or both ears.

hasPart.headline: Symptoms of earache in babies and young children

hasPart.description: Taking painkillers can help ease earache. You can also get treatments like eardrops from a pharmacy.

hasPart.text:
Most earaches get better on their own but get medical help if symptoms do not improve within 2 to 3 days.

Get help sooner if you're worried about other symptoms, such as a high temperature or fluid leaking from the ear.

There are some things you can do to help relieve earache and ear pain.

hasPart.headline: Do
hasPart.text:
• use painkillers, such as paracetamol or ibuprofen (children under 16 should not take aspirin)

  • place a warm flannel on the ear

hasPart.headline: Don't
hasPart.text:
• do not put anything inside your ear, such as cotton buds

  • do not try to remove earwax

  • do not let water get inside your ear

hasPart.headline: Information
hasPart.text: Some painkillers are not safe for everyone (for example, if you're pregnant). Always check the leaflet or get medical advice before taking them.

hasPart.headline: How to treat earache yourself
A pharmacist can help with earaches
hasPart.text:
A pharmacist can tell you:

  • what you can do to treat earache yourself
  • if you can buy anything to help (for example, eardrops)
  • if you need to see a GP
  • if they can treat an infection of the middle ear in children aged 1 to 17

They can provide some treatments if you need it without you seeing a GP.

Find a pharmacy

hasPart.headline: See a GP if:
hasPart.text: • you or your child keep getting earache

hasPart.headline: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if:
hasPart.text:
You or your child have earache and:

  • have had it for more than 2 to 3 days
  • become generally unwell
  • have a very high temperature, or feel hot, cold or shivery
  • have swelling around the ear
  • have fluid coming from the ear
  • have hearing loss or a change in hearing
  • have something stuck in the ear
  • your child is under 2 and has earache in both ears

You can call 111 or get help from 111 online . Call 111 if you need advice for a child under 5 years old.

hasPart.description: Common causes of earache include ear infections, a build-up of earwax in your ear and fluid in your ear (glue ear).

hasPart.text:
Earache and pain is often caused by an ear infection but there are lots of possible causes.

Do not try to diagnose the cause yourself.

hasPart.description: Earache and ear pain is common, particularly in young children. It can be painful but is not usually a sign of anything serious.

hasPart.text: Common causes of earache include ear infections, a build-up of earwax in your ear and fluid in your ear (glue ear).
If you have earache, you may also have other symptoms, such as a high temperature or hearing loss. Earache can be harder to spot in young children.
Taking painkillers can help ease earache. You can also get treatments like eardrops from a pharmacy.

sections.heading: What causes earache and pain
sections.text:
What causes earache and pain
Earache and pain is often caused by an ear infection but there are lots of possible causes.
Do not try to diagnose the cause yourself.
What causes earache and pain
Symptoms
Possible condition
Ear pain with toothache
Children teething, dental abscess
Ear pain with change in hearing
Glue ear, earwax build-up, an object stuck in the ear (do not try to remove it yourself – see a GP), perforated eardrum (particularly after a loud noise or accident)
Ear pain with pain when swallowing
Sore throat, tonsillitis, quinsy (a complication of tonsillitis)
Ear pain with a fever
Ear infection, flu, cold
